body.hook: Push a wall as hard as you can and you do no work on it, yet a gentle push along a slope can change a car's energy. What counts as work?

overview.why: Work is the link between forces and energy, so it turns hard force-and-acceleration problems into simple energy bookkeeping, which IB examiners use constantly. Outside the exam it explains why ramps help, why engines need power ratings and why no machine is perfectly efficient.
learn: Calculate the work done by a constant force using W = Fs cos θ, including when the force is at an angle
Find work done from the area under a force-displacement graph
Apply the work-energy relationship and conservation of mechanical energy to solve motion problems
Use P = Fv and efficiency to analyse energy transfers, including Sankey diagrams and energy density

blocks.title: Why physicists define work
blocks.text: In everyday speech, holding a heavy box feels like work. In physics, work measures energy transferred by a force that moves its point of application. When a crane lifts a 500 kg crate, the crane's force transfers energy to the crate's gravitational potential energy. When friction slows a sliding box, friction transfers kinetic energy to thermal energy. If nothing moves in the direction of the force, no energy is transferred, so no work is done. That is why holding the box still, however tiring for your muscles, does no work on the box.

blocks.title: Need to know
blocks.text: Work done by a force is equivalent to a transfer of energy. Work and energy are both measured in joules (J). One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves its point of application 1 m along the force.

data.statement: A student holds a 5 kg mass stationary at arm's length for one minute. The student does work on the mass because the force is large.
data.right: Correct. The mass does not move, so the displacement is zero and the work done on it is zero.
data.wrong: Work needs displacement along the force. The mass does not move, so W = Fs cos θ = 0, however large the force.

screens.title: The equation W = Fs cos θ

blocks.title: Only the component along the motion counts
blocks.text: A force transfers energy only through the part of it that acts along the displacement. Pulling a suitcase with a strap angled upwards, only the horizontal component of the pull moves the suitcase forward. The vertical component lifts slightly but does not add to the forward motion. If the force F makes an angle θ with the displacement s, the component along s is F cos θ. So the work done is Fs cos θ. For a force of 20 N at 30° over 5.0 m, the work is 20 × 5.0 × cos 30° = 87 J, not 100 J.

blocks.title: Work done by a constant force
A block pulled at an angle
blocks.text: The pulling force F makes 30° with the horizontal displacement. Only its horizontal component does work on the block.

figure.alt: A block on a horizontal surface moving to the right. Weight W acts downward, normal reaction N acts upward from the surface, and a pulling force F acts up and to the right at 30 degrees above the horizontal.

data.prompt: A force of 20 N acts at 30° above the horizontal and pulls a block 5.0 m along a horizontal surface. Calculate the work done by the force.
data.wrong: Use W = Fs cos θ with θ = 30°. Without the cosine you get 100 J; using sin 30° gives 50 J. The correct value is 20 × 5.0 × cos 30° = 87 J.

blocks.title: What the cosine tells you
blocks.text: The sign and size of cos θ tell you what the force does to the energy. If θ = 0°, the force points along the motion, cos θ = 1, and the force adds energy: a push on a trolley speeds it up. If θ = 90°, cos θ = 0, so the force does no work: gravity on a satellite in circular orbit is perpendicular to its motion. If θ = 180°, cos θ = −1 and the work is negative, meaning the force removes energy from the object. Friction on a sliding box does negative work, which is why the box slows down.

data.wrong: A 5.0 kg bag is carried 10 m horizontally at constant velocity, so work by the lifting force = mgs = 490 J.
data.right: The lifting force is vertical and the displacement is horizontal, so θ = 90° and the work done by it is 0.
data.why: Work needs a force component along the displacement. Multiplying force by distance without cos θ ignores the direction of the force.

data.prompt: A person carries a 5.0 kg bag 10 m along a level corridor at constant velocity. What is the work done on the bag by the person's upward lifting force? (g = 9.81 m s^-2)

options.why: This is mgs, which uses the weight and the distance but ignores that the force is perpendicular to the motion.
This is mass × distance, which has no physical meaning here: it uses 5.0 × 10 instead of a force.
Negative work needs a force opposite to the motion (θ = 180°). The lifting force is at 90°, not 180°.

data.right: Correct. The upward force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement, so cos 90° = 0 and W = 0.
data.wrong: The lifting force is vertical and the displacement is horizontal, so θ = 90° and cos θ = 0. The work done is zero.

blocks.title: When the force changes
blocks.text: W = Fs cos θ needs a constant force. Many real forces vary, like the force needed to stretch a spring. In that case, plot the component of force along the motion against displacement. For a tiny displacement the force is nearly constant, so the work is a thin strip of height F and width Δs. Adding all the strips gives the total area under the line. The area under a force-displacement line therefore equals the work done. For a spring with k = 50 N m^-1 stretched from 0 to 0.20 m, the force rises from 0 to 10 N, and the area is a triangle.

blocks.title: Stretching a spring
blocks.text: The line shows force against extension for a spring. The area under the line is the work done in stretching it.

figure.alt: A straight line through the origin showing force in newtons rising linearly with extension in metres, passing through 5 N at 0.10 m and 10 N at 0.20 m.

data.problem: A spring has force constant 50 N m^-1. Calculate the work done in stretching it from rest by 0.20 m.
steps: Force at full extension: F = kx = 50 × 0.20 = 10 N.
The force rises linearly from 0, so the work is the area of a triangle.
W = ½ × base × height = ½ × 0.20 × 10 = 1.0 J.

screens.title: Work done equals change in kinetic energy

blocks.title: The work-energy relationship
blocks.text: When several forces act on an object, add up their work, or equivalently find the work done by the resultant force. This total work equals the change in the energy of the system. If only the kinetic energy changes, the resultant force does work Fs on a mass m, and Fs = ΔEk. A 1200 kg car speeding from 10 m s^-1 to 20 m s^-1 gains ½ × 1200 × (20² − 10²) = 180 000 J. The resultant forward force must have done exactly that much work. This lets you find speeds without using time or acceleration.

symbols.meaning: work done by the resultant force

data.prompt: A resultant force of 6.0 N acts on a 2.0 kg trolley, initially at rest, over a distance of 4.0 m along its motion. Calculate the final speed of the trolley.
data.right: Correct: W = 6.0 × 4.0 = 24 J = ½ × 2.0 × v², so v² = 24 and v = 4.9 m s^-1.
data.wrong: Set the work Fs = 24 J equal to ½mv². Then v² = 2 × 24 / 2.0 = 24, so v = 4.9 m s^-1. Forgetting to take the square root gives 24.

blocks.title: Three stores, one total
blocks.text: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy ½mv², gravitational potential energy mgΔh near the Earth's surface, and elastic potential energy ½k(Δx)². When there is no friction or other resistive force, no energy leaves these stores, so the total is constant and work is just the energy transformed from one form to another. A 0.50 kg ball dropped from 1.8 m loses mgΔh = 8.8 J of potential energy and gains 8.8 J of kinetic energy, giving ½ × 0.50 × v² = 8.8 J and v = 5.9 m s^-1. The mass cancels, so any ball falls at the same speed.

data.expression: $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h \qquad E_H = \frac{1}{2}k(\Delta x)^2 \qquad E_k = \frac{p^2}{2m}$

blocks.title: Think of it like...
blocks.text: Mechanical energy is like money split between a current account, a savings account and a wallet. Moving money between them changes the amounts in each, but the total stays the same unless you spend it on something outside, which is what friction does.

data.prompt: Sort these energy forms into mechanical and not mechanical.

groups.name: Mechanical energy
items: Kinetic energy of a moving trolley
Gravitational potential energy of a raised book
Elastic potential energy of a compressed spring

data.right: Correct. Mechanical energy is only kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy.
data.wrong: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy. Thermal, chemical and nuclear energy are other stores.

blocks.title: Non-conservative forces take mechanical energy
blocks.text: Real motion involves friction and air resistance, so mechanical energy is not conserved. The change in total mechanical energy equals the work done by the non-conservative forces. Consider a 2.0 kg box released from rest at a height of 1.5 m on a rough slope that reaches the bottom at 3.0 m s^-1. It loses mgΔh = 2.0 × 9.81 × 1.5 = 29.4 J of potential energy but gains only ½ × 2.0 × 3.0² = 9.0 J of kinetic energy. The missing 20.4 J is the work done against friction, now thermal energy. Total energy is still conserved.

blocks.title: Need to know
blocks.text: Change in mechanical energy of a system = work done on it by non-conservative forces such as friction. Mechanical energy is lost but total energy is always conserved.

data.prompt: Complete the statement about a box sliding down a rough slope.
data.text: Work done against friction transfers mechanical energy into ___ energy, and the total energy of the system is ___.
data.right: Correct. Friction heats the surfaces, and energy is never destroyed.
data.wrong: Friction transfers mechanical energy to thermal energy. Energy is not destroyed, so the total is conserved.

blocks.title: How fast energy is transferred
blocks.text: Two engines can do the same work, but the one that does it faster is more powerful. Power is the rate of doing work, P = ΔW/Δt. For a force F moving an object at constant speed v along the force, ΔW = FΔs, so P = Fv. A car at a steady 25 m s^-1 against a 600 N resistive force needs 600 × 25 = 15 kW from its engine. Efficiency compares useful output with total input, either as energy or as power. No real machine reaches 1, because some energy is always transferred to thermal energy in the surroundings.

data.expression: $P = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t} = Fv \qquad \eta = \frac{\text{useful power out}}{\text{total power in}}$

symbols.meaning: efficiency (no unit; multiply by 100 for a percentage)

data.prompt: An electric motor takes 500 W of electrical power and lifts a 20 kg load at a constant speed of 0.50 m s^-1. Calculate the efficiency of the motor. Use g = 9.81 m s^-2.
data.right: Correct: useful power = mgv = 20 × 9.81 × 0.50 = 98 W, so η = 98 / 500 = 0.20.
data.wrong: Useful power out is the rate of gain of potential energy: P = Fv = mgv = 98 W. Divide by the input power of 500 W to get 0.20. Dividing 500 by 98 gives 5.1, which is above 1 and impossible.

blocks.title: Showing where energy goes
blocks.text: A Sankey diagram represents energy transfers with arrows whose widths are proportional to the amount of energy. A wide arrow enters the machine and splits into a useful arrow continuing forward and thinner wasted arrows going off to the side. If 200 J enters a lamp and 40 J leaves as light, the useful arrow is one fifth as wide as the input, giving an efficiency of 0.20. Fuels are compared by energy density, the energy released per unit volume or per unit mass. A fuel with higher energy density gives more work from the same amount of fuel.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: The widths of the arrows must add up: input = useful output + wasted output. State units for energy density as J kg^-1 or J m^-3 depending on whether mass or volume is used.

cards.front: What is the equation for work done by a constant force?
cards.back: W = Fs cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement.

cards.front: When is the work done by a force zero?
cards.back: When the displacement is zero or the force is perpendicular to the displacement (θ = 90°).

cards.front: What does the area under a force-displacement graph represent?
cards.back: The work done by the force.
Useful work out / total work in, or useful power out / total power in.

key_terms.definition: The energy transferred when a force moves its point of application; W = Fs cos θ.
The work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m along the direction of the force.
Energy due to motion, ½mv² or p²/2m.
Energy due to position in a gravitational field; near Earth, ΔEp = mgΔh.
Energy stored in a deformed spring, ½k(Δx)².
The sum of kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy.
The rate of doing work or transferring energy; P = ΔW/Δt = Fv.
The ratio of useful work (or power) output to total work (or power) input.
A diagram whose arrow widths are proportional to the energy transferred.
The energy released by a fuel per unit mass or per unit volume.

outcomes.statement: Calculate the work done by a constant force acting at an angle to the displacement.

check.prompt: A force of 40 N acts at 60° to the direction of motion of a trolley that moves 3.0 m. Calculate the work done by the force.
check.wrong: Use W = Fs cos θ = 40 × 3.0 × 0.50 = 60 J. Omitting the cosine gives 120 J.

outcomes.statement: State the relationship between the work done by the resultant force and the change in kinetic energy.

check.statement: The work done by the resultant force on an object equals the change in its energy.
check.right: Correct: net work equals the change in the energy of the system, which is the change in kinetic energy if only kinetic energy changes.
check.wrong: This statement is true: the work done by the resultant force equals the change in the energy of the system.

outcomes.statement: Identify the condition under which the total mechanical energy of a system is conserved.

check.prompt: In which situation is the mechanical energy of the system conserved?

options.text: A ball falls through air with large air resistance
options.why: Air resistance does work, transferring mechanical energy to thermal energy.

options.text: A mass oscillates on a spring in a vacuum with no friction
A box slides down a rough slope
options.why: Friction transfers mechanical energy to thermal energy.

options.text: A car brakes to a halt
options.why: The brakes transfer kinetic energy to thermal energy.

check.right: Correct: with no resistive forces, energy only moves between kinetic and elastic potential energy.
check.wrong: Mechanical energy is conserved only when no frictional or resistive forces do work. Only the spring oscillating in a vacuum fits.

outcomes.statement: Calculate power from force and speed.

check.prompt: A cyclist moves at a constant 8.0 m s^-1 against a total resistive force of 25 N. Calculate the power developed by the cyclist.
check.wrong: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force, so P = Fv = 25 × 8.0 = 200 W. Dividing gives 3.1, which is wrong.

outcomes.statement: Define energy density and state what a Sankey diagram represents.

check.prompt: State what the widths of the arrows in a Sankey diagram are proportional to.
check.right: Correct: arrow width is proportional to the energy transferred.
check.wrong: The width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy being transferred.
